# agent


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

`author(concept, ask)` asks a model for one demo on a concept. The model
writes data only: a JSON spec. It never writes code. Then the loop
checks the spec, and gives the errors back to the model to fix:

1.  Parse the reply as JSON.
2.  [`validate`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/spec.html#validate)
    the spec: types, binds, gates and the think rule.
3.  [`check`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/check.html#check) the
    spec in headless Chrome: it draws, it plays, the keys work, the
    contrast is good.
4.  On errors, ask for a repair with only these errors. At most two
    repairs.
5.  Give up quietly: return `None` and log the errors. The caller keeps
    its text lesson.

`ask(prompt, sp)` is any function that returns text, as in abhyasa. The
tests use a fake one.

## The catalog

The prompt lists the blocks and fns from their manifests, so it never
names a block that the runtime does not have.

``` python
def catalog()->str:
```

*The blocks and fns, with their purpose and props, as text for the
prompt.*

The catalog names every block and every fn.

``` python
cat = catalog()
for n in [*manifests(), *fn_manifests()]: assert f'- {n}: ' in cat, n
print(cat[:600])
```

## The system prompt

The system prompt says who the demo is for, gives the rules of a good
demo, the shape of a spec, and the catalog. The demo is for a human
learner, who can be new to the idea or know it well. A demo that only
restates the definition teaches little. So the prompt asks for a
concrete case first, a picture of it next, and the general rule last
(concreteness fading).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L37"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### demo_sp

``` python
def demo_sp()->str:
```

*The system prompt of the demo agent.*

``` python
assert 'You never write code' in demo_sp() and '- wheel: ' in demo_sp()
assert 'Who this is for' in demo_sp() and 'Never only restate the definition' in demo_sp()
```

## The user prompt

The user prompt describes the concept, the first error of the learner
(if there is one), and two gallery demos as examples. The host can also
give the learner’s `level` as a short text, for example “new to this” or
“knows linear algebra”. With no level, the prompt does not change.
[`near`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#near) picks the
gallery demos that share the most words with the concept. A long table
in an example is cut to three rows.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L67"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### near

``` python
def near(
    concept, k:int=2
)->list:
```

*The `k` gallery demos that share the most words with `concept`.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L78"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### demo_prompt

``` python
def demo_prompt(
    concept, first_error:str='', examples:tuple=(), level:str=''
)->str:
```

*The prompt that asks for a demo on `concept`, a dict with name,
statement, subject and misconceptions.*

``` python
c = dict(name='Reciprocal rank fusion', statement='Sum 1/(k + rank) over the lists.', subject='ml', misconceptions=['raw scores add'])
p = demo_prompt(c, 'You add the raw scores.', near(c))
assert 'first error: You add the raw scores.' in p and '"id": "reciprocal-rank-fusion"' in p
```

A level, when the host gives one, goes into the prompt. With no level,
the prompt is the same as before.

``` python
assert "The learner's level: new to ranking." in demo_prompt(c, level='new to ranking')
test_eq(demo_prompt(c), demo_prompt(c, level=''))
assert 'level' not in demo_prompt(c)
```

## The repair prompt

The repair prompt gives back the spec and only its errors. It tells the
model to keep the teaching text, so a repair does not make the words
more literal.

## author

[`author`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#author) runs
the loop. It stamps the spec with the schema, an id and the concept
slug. `log`, when given, gets one entry for each failed try. `level`
goes on to
[`demo_prompt`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#demo_prompt).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L114"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### author

``` python
def author(
    concept, ask, first_error:str='', examples:NoneType=None, check:bool=True, repairs:int=2, log:list=None,
    level:str=''
)->dict | None:
```

*A checked demo spec on `concept` from the model `ask`, or None after
`repairs` failed repairs. A spec with texts that are not plain
([`plain_errors`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/spec.html#plain_errors))
gets one repair; the plainer good spec stays.*

### Tests with a fake model

`fake` replies from a list, one reply for each call, and keeps the
prompts.

``` python
from rupaka.spec import examples as block_examples
```

``` python
def fake(*replies):
    calls = []
    def ask(p, sp=''): calls.append(p); return replies[min(len(calls), len(replies)) - 1]
    ask.calls = calls
    return ask
good = json.dumps(block_examples()['gate'])
```

A good spec passes on the first call. The spec gets the concept slug.

``` python
a = fake(good)
s = author(dict(name='Sums', slug='sums'), a, check=False)
test_eq((s['concept'], len(a.calls)), ('sums', 1))
```

A spec with one error gets one repair. The repair prompt names the
error.

``` python
broken = json.loads(good); del broken['blocks'][1]['after']
a, log = fake(json.dumps(broken), good), []
s = author('Sums', a, check=False, log=log)
assert s is not None and len(a.calls) == 2
assert 'gives away the answer of gate "sum"' in a.calls[1] and 'Fix only these errors' in a.calls[1]
test_eq(log[0]['tries'], 1)
```

[`author`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#author) gives
the level on to the prompt.

``` python
a = fake(good)
author('Sums', a, check=False, level='an expert')
assert "The learner's level: an expert." in a.calls[0]
```

Three bad replies give up quietly: the result is `None`, and the log has
three entries.

``` python
log = []
test_eq(author('Sums', fake('not json', json.dumps(broken), '{}'), check=False, log=log), None)
test_eq(len(log), 3)
```

A model that fails gives up too, with no exception.

``` python
def down(p, sp=''): raise ConnectionError('no network')
test_eq(author('Sums', down, check=False), None)
```

A good spec with a text that is not plain gets one repair. The repair
prompt names the problem, and the plainer spec comes back.

``` python
vague = json.loads(good); vague['ask'] = 'This departs from the usual rule.'
a, log = fake(json.dumps(vague), good), []
s = author('Sums', a, check=False, log=log)
test_eq((s['ask'], len(a.calls)), (json.loads(good)['ask'], 2))
assert '"departs from" is vague' in a.calls[1]
```

When the repair is not plainer, or does not pass the checks, the first
good spec stays. The plain check never costs a demo.

``` python
test_eq(author('Sums', fake(json.dumps(vague)), check=False)['ask'], vague['ask'])
test_eq(author('Sums', fake(json.dumps(vague), 'not json', 'not json'), check=False)['ask'], vague['ask'])
```

With a browser,
[`check`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/check.html#check) runs
too, and a good spec still passes in one call.

``` python
from rupaka.check import can_check
```

``` python
if can_check(): assert author('Sums', fake(good)) is not None
```

## Plain English

A host can make a text plain with
[`plain`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#plain). When
[`plain_why`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/spec.html#plain_why)
finds problems in a text,
[`plain`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#plain) asks
the model once to write it again, and names the problems. It keeps the
new text only when it has fewer problems and keeps each number, each
`$...$` maths span and each `code` span. Else the old text stays. A text
that passes costs no call. A dict of texts costs at most one call for
all the texts that fail.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L146"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### plain_prompt

``` python
def plain_prompt(
    x, why
)->str:
```

*The prompt that asks the model to write `x` (a text, or a dict of
texts) again; `why` has the problems (of each key, for a dict).*

[`keeps`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#keeps) says
whether a new text keeps the maths, the code and the numbers of the old
text, and each text of `keep` that the old text has.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L156"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### keeps

``` python
def keeps(
    old:str, new:str, keep:tuple=()
)->bool:
```

*Whether `new` has each maths span, code span, number and `keep` text of
`old`.*

``` python
assert keeps('Add $a+b$ to 3 apples.', 'You have 3 apples. Add $a+b$.')
assert not keeps('Add $a+b$ to 3 apples.', 'You have 4 apples. Add $a+b$.')
assert not keeps('Run `f(x)`. Check: why?', 'Run f(x). Check: why?') and not keeps('Check: why?', 'Why?', keep=['Check:'])
```

[`plain`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/agent.html#plain) takes a
text or a dict of texts. A new text must also look like a text: not
empty, not JSON in place of words, and not less than a third of the old
length, and not more than about three times it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/vedicreader/rupaka/blob/main/rupaka/agent.py#L168"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### plain

``` python
def plain(
    ask, x, terms:tuple=(), keep:tuple=()
):
```

*`x` (a text, or a dict of texts) in plain English: each text that fails
[`plain_why`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/spec.html#plain_why)
is written again by `ask` in one call, and kept only when it is better.*

A text that passes makes no call. The owner’s bad question gets one
call, and the plain version comes back.

``` python
good_q = 'In a DDPM, the amount of noise at each step is set before training. Suppose the network learns this amount instead. Which DDPM rule does this break? Why?'
bad_q = 'You train a DDPM on recordings of rain. You ask the network to learn the noise recipe as it trains. Why does this depart from a DDPM simplifying assumption?'
a = fake(good_q)
test_eq((plain(a, good_q), len(a.calls)), (good_q, 0))
test_eq((plain(a, bad_q), len(a.calls)), (good_q, 1))
assert '"recipe" is a nickname' in a.calls[0]
```

A new text that drops a number or the maths, or that is not better, is
not kept. A model that fails keeps the old text too.

``` python
q = 'The loss is $L = (y - 3)^2$; it uses 3 as the target and you facilitate the fit.'
test_eq(plain(fake('The loss is $L$. It uses a target.'), q), q)
test_eq(plain(fake(q), q), q)
test_eq(plain(down, q), q)
new = 'The loss is $L = (y - 3)^2$. It uses 3 as the target. You help the fit.'
test_eq(plain(fake(new), q), new)
```

A dict sends only the texts that fail, in one call, and keeps the others
as they are.

``` python
a = fake(json.dumps(dict(q=good_q)))
test_eq(plain(a, dict(q=bad_q, o='Yes.')), dict(q=good_q, o='Yes.'))
test_eq(len(a.calls), 1); assert '"o"' not in a.calls[0]
```

## A live run

A live run uses a real model, so it is not part of the tests. With the
`rishi` package and its model `claude/sonnet`, it looks like this:

``` python
from rishi import Chat, resp_text
def ask(p, sp=''):
    chat = Chat('claude/sonnet', sp=sp)
    try: return resp_text(chat(p))
    finally: chat.close()
log = []
spec = author(dict(name='Guṇa sandhi', statement='a or ā before i, u or ṛ gives e, o or ar.', subject='sanskrit'), ask, log=log)
```

The first live run (26 October 2026, `claude/sonnet`, three concepts:
guṇa sandhi, cosine similarity and binary search):

So 3 of 3 passed, 2 of them on the first try. One spec put `{n}` in its
plain-text `ask`. The check could not see it, so
[`validate`](https://vedicreader.github.io/rupaka/spec.html#validate)
now refuses a template in a plain-text prop.
